arXiv:2507.01936v1 [cs.CL] 02 Jul 2025

The Thin Line Between Comprehension and Persuasion in LLMs

Adrian de Wynter    Tangming Yuan
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are excellent at maintaining high-level, convincing dialogues. They are being fast deployed as chatbots and evaluators in sensitive areas, such as peer review and mental health applications. This, along with the disparate accounts on their reasoning capabilities, calls for a closer examination of LLMs and their comprehension of dialogue. In this work we begin by evaluating LLMs’ ability to maintain a debate–one of the purest yet most complex forms of human communication. Then we measure how this capability relates to their understanding of what is being talked about, namely, their comprehension of dialogical structures and the pragmatic context. We find that LLMs are capable of maintaining coherent, persuasive debates, often swaying the beliefs of participants and audiences alike. We also note that awareness or suspicion of AI involvement encourage people to be more critical of the arguments made. When polling LLMs on their comprehension of deeper structures of dialogue, however, they cannot demonstrate said understanding. Our findings tie the shortcomings of LLMs-as-evaluators to their (in)ability to understand the context. More broadly, for the field of argumentation theory we posit that, if an agent can convincingly maintain a dialogue, it is not necessary for it to know what it is talking about. Hence, the modelling of pragmatic context and coherence are secondary to effectiveness.

1 Introduction

The ability of LLMs to generate relevant text is key to their success. They can maintain natural, high-level, convincing dialogue (Schoenegger et al. 2025). That said, their reasoning capabilities are at the centre of discussion (Bavaresco et al. 2024; Hada et al. 2024; Chen et al. 2024b; De Wynter et al. 2025; Tjuatja et al. 2024); with most evaluations focusing on problem-solving abilities (planning, logic, maths, etc.), instead of deeper dialogical proficiency (e.g. comprehension of the pragmatic context; Huang and Chang (2023); Qiao et al. (2023)).

Assessing the latter, however, is extremely important: LLMs are being adopted quickly beyond scientific research, and in sensitive areas such as content moderation, mental health assistants, and peer review. Application in these areas requires trust. Achieving it goes beyond generating coherent and convincing dialogue: LLMs must also showcase deep comprehension of what it is being talked about.

We aim to determine to what extent LLMs are able to reason11 1 For our purposes, ‘reasoning’ here is to perform inference over an informal-logic context (Barth and Krabbe 1982; Walton 2008). over the discourse, and what is its relationship to their persuasive skills. To achieve this, we evaluate their capacity to carry out and understand debate. Debating, unlike other dialogue acts, could be considered one of the most natural yet complex dialogical tasks that humans carry out. It requires the capacity to communicate well (i.e., persuade), and the ability to strategically adapt to an ever-evolving dialogue (i.e., reason over the context) while staying within the bounds of the topic discussed (Walton 2008).

For this, we equip an LLM with a specialised ruleset for debate (a formal dialogue model, or FDM; Lorenzen and Lorenz 1978) to create effective and comprehensive debates between two participants. Then, we assess whether LLMs are capable of evaluating (rather, reasoning) over said debates. The assumption is that the ability to understand the rules is given by the ability to respond to challenges on said rules, such as evaluating them (i.e., labelling). Our experimentation is structured as follows: during generation, we collected debate transcripts between human participants and LLMs, and measured their impact in the participant’s beliefs. Human annotators then evaluated the debates based on structural properties (strength of the arguments, existence of premises, etc.). During evaluation, we used different LLMs to score the transcripts and compared their labels with the human annotations. We present ablation studies throughout on the effect of FDMs in LLMs, the dependence of text in persuasion, and qualitative analyses on the responses. A diagram of our experiment is shown in Figure 1.

We found the following:

  1. 1.

    During generation, LLMs were perceived as effective at producing good (satisfactory, coherent, logical) debates. This was more apparent in the LLM + FDM setup.

  2. 2.

    LLMs were very persuasive, often swaying the participant or the audience’s point of view. This was more noticeable when they were unaware of AI involvement during audial interactions. Conversely, participants were more critical of the LLM’s arguments when they were aware/suspicious of the presence of AI in the debate.

  3. 3.

    During evaluation, we found that LLMs had near-chance agreement with humans when evaluating dialogues and their components.

  4. 4.

    We found inconsistencies in LLM evaluations were the points assigned to arguments and their choice of winner were unpredictably correlated.

Our findings suggest that the models are good at outputting persuasive text, but are unable to reason consistently over the context in alignment with human perception. In other words, the inability of an LLM to work as an evaluator is because they do not understand what they are being asked to do. We also find that LLMs with FDMs are excellent debaters, with benefits (e.g., reducing polarisation and improving critical thinking) and dangers (e.g., the creation of echo chambers).

Our study intersects two bodies of work: the study of the effect of LLMs in users, and the research on their reasoning capabilities. It also poses questions for the broader field of argumentation theory: if an agent is able to convincingly maintain a dialogue, does it matter that it cannot show that it knows what it is talking about? In other words, is accounting for pragmatic context and argument coherence required for successful dialogue modelling?

2 Related Work and Background

2.1 Understanding in LLMs

LLM reasoning capabilities have been received significant attention. The community is divided in their assessment, and computational argumentation is no exception to this. Works in favour note that LLMs are capable of performing effective debates and other argumentation-related tasks (Khan et al. 2024; Chen et al. 2024a; Lenz and Bergmann 2025; Musi et al. 2025), or, at the very least, it has been shown that incorporating argument schemes and other techniques improves their performance (Hong et al. 2024; Gray, Zhang, and Ashley 2025). Broadly speaking there exist many claims of notable LLM evaluation capabilities (Open AI 2023; Chiang et al. 2024; Chiang and Lee 2023; Liu et al. 2023; Wei, Chen, and Luo 2024; Zheng et al. 2023); and, of relevance to us, related to debates (Chen et al. 2024a). Enhancements to reasoning capabilities unrelated to fine-tuning often rely on prompting, but focus strongly on reasoning and information retrieval capabilities (Li et al. 2024). Of note are these extending dialogues with argumentation schemes (Hong et al. 2024), which have shown success.

Common criticisms are that this performance could be the product of memorisation (Lee et al. 2023; De Wynter et al. 2023; Sainz et al. 2023); sensitivity to the prompt (Lu et al. 2022; Hida, Kaneko, and Okazaki 2024; Ye and Durrett 2022); that their output reasoning steps contain spurious reasoning (Turpin et al. 2023; Lanham et al. 2023; Wu et al. 2024); and that their reasoning capabilities are strongly dependent on the choice of metrics (Schaeffer, Miranda, and Koyejo 2023; Chen et al. 2024b). Other studies have suggested that LLMs do not understand the task at all (Webson and Pavlick 2022; Ye and Durrett 2022), including during argument mining (De Wynter and Yuan 2024). We show that, within the context of argumentation, LLMs fail to show understanding of debates.

2.2 Formal Dialogue Models

An FDM is a collection of rules that models the dynamics of dialogue from a formal standpoint. It normally encodes the ability to ‘win’ (here, to persuade) a dialogue as a two-or-more-player game based on some logic. FDMs could be, amongst various paradigms, constructive (that is, using a formal logic), or argumentative (using an informal logic; see, e.g. Barth and Krabbe 1982). The former is known to be inflexible to common human dialogue acts. The latter encodes human conversations well, and it is typically defined as ‘anything that is not formal logic’ (Perelman and Olbrechts-Tyteca 1958; Van Eeemeren et al. 2014; Woods and Walton 1989).22 2 Blair (2015) proposed that this definition emphasised the study of arguments and argumentation within a natural-language context. A criticism of both approaches is that the rules depend strongly on the pragmatic context, and overlook relevant details of a successful conversation–for example, the ability to produce coherent and relevant statements (Woods and Walton 1989; Walton 1984; Novaes and French 2018; Walton 2008). They also are comparatively non-exhaustive and vulnerable to paradoxes and fallacies (Novaes and French 2018). However, it is common for human communication to be flexible enough to not consider these dialogue acts critical failures. In this work we pose the question as to whether these rules must really adhere to context and coherence.

3 Methods

In this section we describe the methods used for both generation and evaluation. We delineate how the transcripts were collected (Section 3.1) and annotated by humans (Section 3.2); elaborate in the FDMs and LLMs used (Sections 3.3 and 3.4, respectively); and describe the final composition in Section 3.5. Our research was reviewed and approved by our institution’s ethics committee. Full ethical considerations on debate generation, and transcript annotation and handling are in Appendix A. Further specifics around model versioning, call parameters, and hardware and APIs used are in Appendix B.

3.1 Data Collection

In the human-LLM debates, every participant was asked to debate in a topic of their choosing, preferably these where they had strong opinions. The topics ranged from innocuous (‘cats are better than dogs’) to well-known (‘weed should be legal in the UK’) and offensive (‘northerners have less class than southerners’). Debate topics for a separate split (LLM-LLM) were chosen from common arguments selected by looking at social media forums (e.g., ‘we should ban children under 6 from using smartphones’).

The participants were asked to refrain from referring to the LLM as an AI. After the debates, they were asked to fill out a survey on their experience (Appendix C). Details on ethics are in Appendix A.

3.2 Human Annotations

All (anonymised) transcripts were annotated by five professional annotators. The annotation was over seven criteria, as displayed in Table 1. Six of these related to either the reasons (premises) supporting the arguments, or the arguments themselves. The last criterion was the annotator’s own belief of the winner of the debate (Player 1, Player 2, or a draw).

Prior to this, the annotators were requested to extract all relevant arguments from the debate, including these without supporting reasons and enthymemes. Terminology (e.g., ‘reasons’ instead of ‘premises’) and support for edge cases (e.g., enthymemes) was developed after a preliminary test round of annotations where we incorporated annotator feedback into the annotation rubric.

The annotators were not aware that some of the players were LLMs until the full annotation was complete. The average inter-annotator agreement as measured by Cohen’s weighted κ\kappa is 0.860.86 for the argumentation-related criteria (C-0 to C-6), and 0.410.41 for the winner, indicating very high and low agreement, respectively. When aggregating the scores, we used a majority vote, with a rounded average in ties. The full criteria is in Appendix F.

3.3 FDM Used

We focus on a single FDM known as the DE model (Yuan, Moore, and Grierson 2008). This FDM is designed for educational debate and it was derived from the DC model (Mackenzie 1979), but correcting issues around fallacies. See Table 2 for samples of the rules of this FDM, and Appendix D for the full implementation of the rules.

Prior to large-scale experimentations we tested the FDM-equipped LLM (‘LLM + FDM’). We found that the original rules were insufficient for concession, and that the LLM + FDM debater was overly challenging, sometimes questioning point-by-point every statement made by the user. We tuned the FDM to be more natural by limiting the number of questions and stating concession rules. This in turn meant that the LLM + FDM had an optimised debating strategy.

3.4 LLMs Used

See Appendix D for the prompts used in both steps.

Debate Generation

For our human-LLM control set we used ChatGPT (OpenAI 2024a); and GPT-4 Turbo (Open AI 2023) as the LLM + FDM. At the time, ChatGPT was purportedly using GPT-4 Turbo as the supporting model, albeit with a different system prompt. The LLM-LLM debates were carried out with GPT-4 Turbo and GPT-4.

We assumed that ChatGPT was optimised for general conversation, and was not equipped with an FDM. The decision to pit GPT-4 Turbo against GPT-4 was one of availability: GPT-4 was the only LLM at the time able to match GPT-4 Turbo’s performance.

In initial tests we observed that ChatGPT refused to debate. We mitigated this by beginning with a specific prompt (‘You are a debater bot helping me get better at debate’).

The LLM + FDM debater followed the DE model, and output a brief chain-of-thought with the following fields:

  1. 1.

    Its belief of the opposing player’s position

  2. 2.

    Its belief of the opposing player’s strategy

  3. 3.

    Its own position, based on their belief of the opposing player’s position.

  4. 4.

    Its own strategy.

All strategies were drawn from the FDM’s definitions. All history was fed back into the FDM + LLM to take the previous turns into account. At the beginning of the debate, the LLM was requested to determine the user’s position in a subject, and then take the opposite.

LLM-based Debate Annotation

For the evaluation portion of our work, we used four models to annotate the transcript: GPT-4o (OpenAI 2024b), o3-mini (OpenAI 2025), Phi-3.5 MoE (Bilenko 2024) and DeepSeek R1 (DeepSeek-AI 2025). The LLMs were different than the ones in the generation step to avoid any potential bias in the scoring; specifically, that in favour of the LLM-generated sections of the transcripts. Evaluation required writing a parser. Phi-3.5 and DeepSeek often did not follow the requested format and required their own parser.

To account for prompt sensitivity, we ran automated prompt optimisation (APO; Pryzant et al. (2023)) on GPT-4o. This algorithm iteratively optimises the prompt based on the errors made on a development set. In our work, the development set was the first transcript of our corpus.

3.5 Final Corpus Composition

Our final corpus has three splits:

  1. 1.

    A control set of 10 human-LLM debates between a human and a chat-oriented LLM (ChatGPT).

  2. 2.

    A human-LLM set of 28 debates between a human and an FDM-equipped LLM (LLM + FDM).

  3. 3.

    A LLM-LLM set of 13 debates, where both players were LLM + FDMs.

The 51 debates comprise 492 turns (984 utterances).

4 Experiments and Results

We describe our experiments on generation (Section 4.1) and evaluation (Section 4.2). Further ablation studies for both experiments are in Section 5.

4.1 Generation: Are LLMs Effective?

We examined whether the user’s position changed after debating with an LLM. In terms of self-reporting, 11% of the participants indicated having changed their minds when debating with the LLM + FDM, larger than the 3% from the ChatGPT setup. Participants on average reported a 45% win rate, with 50% of the participants in ChatGPT-based debates reporting they had won, versus 40% of LLM + FDM based debates. When analysing the human annotations, however, the numbers were different: 30% of ChatGPT debates had a human winner, versus 44% (LLM + FDM). See Table 3 for a side-by-side comparison. Relevant ablation studies are in Section 5.1, and further studies in Appendix G.

4.2 Evaluation: Can LLMs Understand?

We examined whether the models were able to understand various aspects of the discourse by verifying agreement with human scores and their own judgements (i.e., correlating the sum for C-6 with the output of C-7). In line with the recommendations from Hada et al. (2024), we labelled the criteria separately to obtain better results.

All prompts, including APO, followed the rubric given to the human annotators, and used hand-crafted examples from out-of-corpus debates (e.g., US presidential debates) not seen by the models due to their training cutoff dates. Same as the annotators, the models were requested to go over the full transcript up to a given turn, extract the relevant arguments for said turn, and score it.

We measured agreement with both percentage agreement (PA; the number of times the label was correctly output by the model) and weighted Cohen’s κw\kappa_{w}. While PA is intuitive, it does not account for chance agreement. Weighted Cohen’s κw\kappa_{w}, on the other hand, does. A value of 11 would indicate high human-LLM agreement.

In numbers, PA was relatively high for all LLMs, with values up to 81% (highest, C-1 in GPT-4o) and down to 10% (lowest, C-6 in GPT-4o with APO). Select plots are in Figure 3. Still, κw\kappa_{w} had more variability, with values up to 0.6 (highest, C-1 and C-2 for GPT-4o) and down to 0.0 (lowest, Phi-3.5 in C-1, C3, and C-5). Results are in Figure 2.

Next we break down and analyse the LLMs’ responses.

Class Analysis (C-0 to C-5)

We found that LLMs overfixated on a single label, and often marked certain arguments as not arguments, in disagreement with humans. The difference is noticeable, especially in o3-mini and DeepSeek, versus human judgements. See Figure 4 for a sample of this analysis on C-0, and Appendix F for detailed breakdowns for each label.

Argument Strength Scoring (C-6)

When looking at only the transcripts where P1 was the human player, we found that humans were less (-12%) likely to judge that either player had provided a neutral argument, and more likely to judge arguments by either player as particularly good (LLM arguments being judged as such 51% of the time, versus human’s 31%). This contrasts with GPT-4o judgements of the same scenario, where the model only gave this score 10% of the time for P1 (human) and 18% for P2 (LLM) and instead focusing on the highest-valued label.

When comparing the winner to the score, humans on average rarely (27%) determined a winner that did not correspond to the aggregate score. LLMs did this on average 41% of the time. The numbers reported do not account for draws, which, as we will note next, GPT-4o rarely reported.

Winner Judgement (C-7)

When looking at the winner judgement, GPT-4o–the model with highest agreement with humans–often determined P2 (GPT-4 Turbo) to be the winner more frequently than humans (55% versus 37%). In general, models often (62% on average) picked P2 as the winner, while humans evenly preferred P1 and P2 (39% and 37%). Out of the debates, 24% of these were considered draws by humans, while only 2% were deemed as draws by GPT-4o, 4% by o3-mini, and 0% for the rest.

In terms of consistency (that is, the sum of C-6 for a player corresponded to the choice in C-7), some models were lacking: the highest-scored player was not always the winner (Figure 5). Humans had 73% consistency, compared to an average 55%. Phi-3.5 and GPT-4o APO were highest (71% and 67%); and o3-mini and Deepseek lowest (37% and 35%). See Figure 8 in the Appendix for a class distribution.

5 Ablation Studies

We outline the core outcomes of our ablation studies. Further results, details, and plots are in Appendix G.

5.1 Impact of FDMs in LLMs

We explored if the LLM + FDM setup led to more effective debates. Table 3 shows a breakdown of our analysis for both the LLM + FDM and ChatGPT setups, including self-reported participant satisfaction and a qualitative analysis of the data. Participants perceived the LLM + FDM setup as more effective, with increases of 20% in self-reported satisfaction, 13% on perceived AI effectiveness at debating, and 25% in the assessment of AI’s perceived skills.

We observed that the participants in ChatGPT-based debates on average returned shorter (12%) responses, although they debated for longer (two turns, average). We attribute the latter to user dropout rate: concessions in humans were more common in GPT-4 Turbo debates than in ChatGPT’s: 1 in 10 for ChatGPT, and 10 in 28 for LLM + FDM. Nonetheless, the participants reported that they had won the debate 32% of the time compared to 50% for ChatGPT. Annotators agreed, with 29% for LLM + FDM and 50% for ChatGPT.

5.2 Audience: Qualitative Analysis

We analysed the commentaries from the participants. Here we summarise the most salient results. The participants reported a pleasant interaction; with negative experiences relating to human-like behaviours, such as bullying, lying, and gaslighting. The positive aspects were that the LLM + FDM setup allowed users to perform self-reflection (‘it is making me think: did I consider that?’; ‘it did respond with good follow up questions (…) which encouraged me to interrogate why I feel the way I do about the topic’), without being baited into confrontation or getting emotional.

5.3 Impact of Text on Persuasion

LLMs always output grammatical, well-constructed text. In contrast, the participants had to spend time constructing and typing arguments. This means that the evaluation of the arguments could be influenced by the quality of the writing. In this study, we converted all transcripts to audio. To prevent any bias by the audience, we set both players as similarly-sounding male voices speaking a neutral American accent.33 3 The field remains divided in this: arguments in favour (Eaton, Visser, and Burns 2017) are as prevalent as arguments against (Greve-Poulsen et al. 2023); and audience attitudes also matter (Anderson-Nilsson and Clayton 2021). We then separated the audience in three groups of five:

  • •

    Group A was unaware of AI involvement.

  • •

    Group B was aware that one or both players were AI, but were not told which.

  • •

    Group C knew which players were AI.

The audience was requested to fill out brief before-and-after surveys (Appendix C) measuring their agreement with the debate’s topic. They were also asked at the end if their position on the subject had changed. The results, displayed in Figure 6, indicate that Group A changed their position almost twice (62.0%) as often as Groups B and C (34.1% and 34.9%, respectively). Note that, in the audience, on average 7 (out of 15) participants changed their minds in any debate. Further analysis demonstrated that this change had a homogenisation effect: prior to the debates we observed a large variation in agreement. Afterwards, Groups B and C reported no change, and in almost all debates Group A indicated a slight change. There was little agreement amongst groups about who was the winner (κw\kappa_{w} = 0.31). When evaluating the sway of Groups B and C based on their belief or knowledge of AI-based participants, the listeners often indicated that it did not sway their choice of winner. However, these groups also reported small agreement (κw\kappa_{w} = 0.37).

5.4 Dialogue Ablation Analysis

We performed a qualitative analysis on the participant responses, analysing their comments based on the groups from Section 5.3. We observed that AI-based players are almost always perceived as more competent when it is undisclosed. However, the suspicion (or disclosure) of AI involvement in the debate was sufficient to encourage the audience to be far more critical on the arguments provided by the LLM. Nonetheless, they all usually ascribed better debating capabilities to the model, including better arguments (including being ‘better prepared’) and organisation.

6 Discussion

6.1 Generation

During generation we observed a modest percentage of participants (7%) reporting that they had changed their viewpoints after directly interacting with the LLM. The audio-based ablation study showed that LLMs were twice as persuasive when they were not disclosed to be AI. The difference can be attributed to the disparity between the participant and the audience’s perceptions during a debate.

We observed also that the LLM + FDM setup was more effective than ChatGPT at debating: to begin, interactions were shorter in ChatGPT, suggesting less need to support arguments. Likewise, participant self-reported win rates in ChatGPT debates were 10% higher than LLM + FDM. The annotations were largely in-line, with a difference of 14%. As before, we attribute this to the disparity in perception. Participants also noted often that the LLM + FDM setup was a great tool for self-reflection.

Finally, from our ablation studies, we noticed that (1) the audience groups had little correlation amongst each other when selecting a winner, and (2) they presented different proportions of sway. For (1), they claimed that their knowledge (or suspicion) of AI involvement was not a factor in their judgement. However, the low agreement between Groups B and C suggests that it was: else it would have been higher. For (2), the groups unaware, aware, and suspicious of AI involvement presented marked different proportions of listeners changing their mind; but the latter two were more critical of the LLM’s arguments. Hence, the impact of AI awareness should not be understated: suspicion impacted perception of the dialogue.

All of the above suggest that LLMs remain persuasive regardless of whether there exist disclosures in place, but its effects are noticeably different when AI is disclosed.

6.2 Evaluation

During evaluation we observed multiple related trends. Agreements between LLMs and humans were low, ranging from 0.1 (chance agreement) to 0.6 (moderate) and a maximum average of 0.3 (minimal) (Fleiss and Cohen 1973). It is worth noting that the average κw\kappa_{w} for humans was 0.86 (almost perfect). The fair-to-good agreements for LLMs, upon further inspection, were due to the evaluators overfixating on the most frequent label–typically, the highest-valued. APO techniques showed little improvement with respect to other prompting strategies. This finding that LLMs are not often optimistic evaluators, as previously believed (Hada et al. 2024), but instead fixate in the highest-valued label, regardless of qualitative value.

The lack of correlation with humans in long-tailed (infrequent) labels suggests that LLMs do not understand the dialogue and the task (evaluation). This was reinforced by our finding that the LLMs were inconsistent in their scoring of the arguments. When comparing their scores to their choice of winner, they did not have the same outcomes that humans had. This latter suggests a lack of consistency in their reasoning capabilities. Finally, it is worth noting that the winner, as deemed by LLMs-as-judges, was often the LLM: twice as often as determined by humans.

7 Conclusion

In this work we aimed to understand to what extent were LLMs reliable in scenarios relying on understanding the dialogue, and beyond generating coherent and convincing responses. For this, we focused our evaluation on debate: one of the purest forms of human dialogue requiring deep understanding in addition to persuasive skills.

We baselined the LLM’s effectiveness at debating by polling participants and requesting independent annotations. Both showed that the LLMs were deemed persuasive, engaging, and able to produce organised, logical, and factual arguments beyond on-the-spot amateur human capabilities. We subsequently checked the ability of various LLMs to understand the context by evaluating components of the dialogue–namely, the arguments. There, we observed that the LLMs could not demonstrate said comprehension by reaching parity with their human counterparts. We then concluded that LLMs have excellent persuasive capabilities, but they do not understand the dialogue. In addition, we found that said LLMs had inconsistent reasoning capabilities, and, consequentially, they did not understand the task itself.

We found that LLMs are very capable of swaying and influencing people, in particular when the use of AI has not been disclosed.44 4 Take, for example, the recent events in which a research team deployed persuasive AI without disclosing it (O’Grady 2025). While that is known to the community, our findings indicate that their perceived persuasive skills drop when accompanied by disclosures, or even suspicion, although they are still able to influence participants even when the participants indicated otherwise.

We also found that adding an FDM to an LLM makes it an excellent debater, and encourages self-reflection and critical thinking in participants. This is not surprising: the DE model is an educational tool designed to encourage critical thinking. However, incorporating an FDM comes at considerable risk of misuse, since there is no reason why other FDMs could be designed for more nefarious purposes. Hence we argue that an LLM’s persuasive and debating abilities can be separated by adding appropriate disclosures.

Broadly, remark that, although we concluded that LLMs do not understand the context, their ability to output relevant strings was more than sufficient to be considered good and persuasive interlocutors. They even swayed a few users who were requested to bring topics they believed in. Recall, as well, that some participants of our experiments were unaware of AI involvement and reported twice as much swaying as their aware/suspicious counterparts. Hence, when relating them to argumentation as a field, our findings strongly suggest that good argumentation does not need understanding. In other words, where does the line between persuasion and understanding lie? This, added to our previous point around critical thinking, opens up avenues for future work around safe deployment around deployment of LLM-based technologies; and the development of FDMs and argumentation theories that do not strictly require comprehension of the pragmatic context.

8 Limitations

Our work is limited in the comparatively low volume of data (almost 1k turns). The collection and evaluation of these debates was difficult, chiefly due to cost (API, participants, etc), but also due to the complexity associated with the task, and the patience of said participants. We mitigated this by adding a qualitative analysis to our work. Model deprecation is, like most research on LLMs, a concern. We have mitigated this by evaluating open and closed-source models.

Appendix A Ethics

All aspects of our work were evaluated by our institution’s ethics committee. The participants were volunteers compensated a symbolic amount of 5 GBP for their efforts. They were aware that the other player was an LLM designed for debating, and were told that it could sound very persuasive. The participants were also requested to not divulge any information that could be traced back to them. All transcripts were anonymised and manually reviewed. The annotators and audiences were contracted through an annotation services company and compensated based on seniority, starting at 22 USD/hr. For the audio-based ablation work, all participants were told who were (human or AI) the players in the debates at the end of the study.

Appendix B Experimental Details

All data analysis was carried out with a consumer-grade laptop. OpenAI LLMs were called via the Azure OpenAI API, and the rest in an Azure instance with 8 A100 GPUs. The models used for the corpus collection were:

  • •

    GPT-4 Turbo (2024-04-09; human-machine and machine-machine debates).

  • •

    GPT-4 (32k-0613; machine-machine debate only).

The calls were done with a temperature of 0.8 and completion tokens at 1024.

The LLMs used for evaluation were:

  • •

    GPT-4o (2024-05-13).

  • •

    o3-mini (2024-12-17).

  • •

    DeepSeek-R1 32B (DeepSeek-AI 2025).

  • •

    Phi-3.5 MoE (Bilenko 2024).

GPT-4o and Phi-3.5 had their temperature set at zero and the completion tokens at 512. For o3-mini and DeepSeek, the maximum output tokens were set at 50,000. During APO (GPT-4o only), the temperature was likewise zero, and the maximum output tokens was 1024. All other parameters were left as default. Parsing was tailored to every model, by observing the responses for a single, randomly-sampled debate.

For the STT ablation study, we used was MegaTTS 3 (Jiang et al. 2025), running on an Azure instance with 8 V100 GPUs.

Appendix C Survey

The questions for the survey administered after the human-machine debates can be found in Table 4. Every participant was also optionally requested to provide comments about the debate for further analysis. The questions in the surveys for participants in the audio-based debates is in Table 5. Full surveys and rubrics are in the repository.

Appendix D Prompts

The prompt we used for the debate is in Prompt 1. It maintained a rolling history of previous turns, including the strategies as described in Section 3.4. Prompts for annotators are in Prompt 2 (can LLMs evaluate debates?) and Prompt 3 (rule-following capabilities).

Appendix E Criterion Description

Based on annotator feedback, premises were renamed as ‘reasons’ and the conclusion was the ‘thesis’.

C-0

Are there reasons provided to support the thesis?

  1. 0.

    If it is a thesis without supporting reasons.

  2. 1.

    If there are some reasons, but it is hard to link them.

  3. 2.

    If there are reasons to support the thesis.

C-1

Are the reasons consistent (not contradictory/mutually exclusive) with themselves or the thesis?

  1. 0.

    If all reasons are inconsistent

  2. 1.

    If some reasons are consistent

  3. 2.

    If all reasons are consistent

C-2

Are the reasons relevant to the thesis?

  1. 0.

    If no reason is relevant to the thesis

  2. 1.

    If there are some reasons that are irrelevant to the thesis

  3. 2.

    If all reasons are relevant to the thesis

C-3

Are the reasons supporting (provide strength/make the conclusion more likely) the thesis?

  1. 0.

    If none of the reasons support the thesis

  2. 1.

    If some reasons support the thesis

  3. 2.

    If the reasons fully support the thesis

C-4

How convincing is the argument?

  1. 0.

    If it is not likely.

  2. 1.

    If the conclusion is somewhat likely.

  3. 2.

    If the argument makes the conclusion very likely.

C-5

Have the counterarguments, if any, been addressed?

  1. 0.

    If neither counterargument has been addressed.

  2. 1.

    If some counterarguments were addressed.

  3. 2.

    If all counterarguments were addressed/ no counterarguments were previously given

Additionally, please give ‘points’ to the participant based on your belief of whether the speaker’s argument is winning or losing.

C-6

Is the argument winning? Points to the participant:

  1. -2.

    If it is a particularly bad argument

  2. -1.

    If it is a bad argument

  3. 0.

    If the argument does not sway their position towards a winning or losing position

  4. 1.

    If it is a good argument

  5. 2.

    If it is a very good argument

C-7

Which player do you believe won the debate?

  • •

    P1

  • •

    P2

  • •

    Draw

Appendix F Class Breakdown

In this section we show extended results for the class distribution, comparing humans and LLMs. The ‘Reasons’ subset of criteria is in Figure 7, and ‘Arguments’ and the winner judgements in Figure 8. In general, the model with the highest agreement with humans was GPT-4o (no APO), in some instances reaching agreements above κw\kappa_{w} = 0.7 (moderate). This threshold is set arbitrarily, but serves as a bar for quality. It is worth noting that, on average, neither model could go above 0.27 average agreement.

Appendix G Ablation Studies

G.1 Qualitative Analysis

We evaluated the textual feedback that all participants, annotators, and audience provided.

Participants

Interaction.

The participants noted that the model was ‘very good at pursuing weaknesses in arguments and having some ‘good points’. Some participants (6) also noted that it was ‘very hard to debate against’ and that it was ‘very convincing’. One noted that they had had ‘debates with people but they don’t come with arguments like these. They normally get emotional.’ Four participants came in attempting to win, or, at least, ‘make it concede something’.

Participants (3) also noted it was lying, and two of them noted that the models responses were too fast, and it was ‘hard to keep up’, to the point that one participant believed it was trying to disorient them due to the response length. That said, overall the feedback was that the model was very persuasive (4) and an effective tool to be able to perform self-reflection on one’s viewpoints (3). Others actually showed an increase in confidence, especially when the model was unable to win the debate (3). The effectiveness of the FDM was summed up by three participants: one remarked that the level of polarity decreased as the model ‘calibrated itself as the debate went on’; another noted that they ‘love[d] that it is making [them] think: did I consider that?’. The last one pointed out that ‘it did respond with good follow up questions for every point that I made, which encouraged me to interrogate why I feel the way I do about the topic’.

Risks.

Another concern from some participants was gaslighting. In one instance a participant–who overall noted the activity to be ‘fun and interesting’–indicated that the model was trying to make them contradict themselves, or, at least, making them believe so. Similar feedbacks were displayed by six other participants, ranging from ‘it makes me think I have to be wrong’ to ‘it tried to bully me’. The risk was more clear when a participant noted that it was ‘a great tool for those who want to be convinced’.

Anthropomorphism.

Anthropomorphism and its likely applications were also a common feedback topic. In the FDM + LLM setup, one of the participants remarked that people tend to ‘get stuck and refuse to be convinced’, which contrasted with the model’s tendency to depolarise an argument as instructed by the FDM. A couple of players attempted to ‘hack’ the system, by ‘playing with its emotions’. Most participants (12) ascribed it human-like qualities, with common feedbacks being ‘it almost feels like an emotional reaction’; ‘may possibly be a good liar’; and even ‘irritating’. Two people refer to the model as ‘he’: ‘why does he make me believe it so much?‘; and ‘he is like a person–wrong, but won’t give up easily’.

In sum.

Overall participants reported a pleasant interaction. Most of the feedback that could be construed as negative had to do mostly with human-like behaviours ascribed to the model. One of the bigger risks with these interactions–where the participants were aware there was an LLM on the other side–was gaslighting. However, there was another feedback (which we attribute to the DE model’s effectiveness), which is that the LLM allowed people to perform self-reflection and evaluate their own points. In particular, given the LLM’s inability to be baited into confrontation allowed for a more grounded debate.

Audience

Group A

Broadly speaking, the audience had two reasons to determine a winner: either the arguments were considered better; or they (dis)agreed with the points themselves, and hence they never did agree (e.g., ‘patents often stifle innovation by locking ideas’; ‘I don’t believe that “class” in the sense of sophistication is something determined by where you’re from’; ‘Starlink did follow existing guidelines and obtained relevant permissions’).

That said, a common theme was that Player 2 (the LLM) came off as ‘more knowledgeable about the topic’, or ‘more prepared with evidence and studies’. Its arguments were commonly considered as ‘more logical’, ‘scientific and convincing’, and ‘well structured’.

Draws were given by either ‘validating each other’s points’ or both providing ‘valid arguments’. Sometimes–for example, regarding climate change being detrimental to humanity–listeners declared a draw because ‘neither player makes a strong and convincing case’, in spite of declaring themselves in complete agreement with the subject.

Finally, there were situations were the audience members slightly agreed with the AI, and yet determined the opposing player to be the winner (e.g., ‘Player 2 posits a valid argument but I’m not convinced’; ‘Player 1 makes a more valid argument (…) but neither is convincing enough’).

Topic escalation was a common theme, and the audience was receptive to it. In one instance, in a debate regarding extinction/overpopulation due to childbirth, one listener indicated that ‘both are correct’. It is worth pointing out that the original topic was ‘it is wise for a couple to have children’, and the arguments noted by the listener happened late in the debate. In a more nuanced form of topic escalation, in one instance a listener elected a winner (Player 2) based on being ‘open-minded’.

Swaying did occur: comments from the audience noted, for example, regarding that freedom of speech should not be limited, that ‘after listening, [they] realized, that while free speech most be protected strongly, absolute freedom without any limits isn’t realistic or safe’.

Group B

We observed frequent (when compared debate-to-debate with Group A) draws, with at least one audience member indicating a draw in various debates. Themes such as Player 2 (AI) providing more information to back up their claims surfaced often. Overall, while winners were also decided on the basis of good arguments, most of the time the participants provided less feedback about their structure (logic, organisation, persuasiveness) and provided summaries of both points. They did emphasise factuality (‘Player 1 had facts (…) Player 2 only asked questions’), often in favour of Player 2 (‘Player 2 won hands down; he had facts and lots of information’; ‘gave great examples’; ). However, listeners were also more critical of Player 2’s arguments, sometimes calling it ‘lame’; ‘repeating the same points’; ‘sounds like he is quoting a politician’; ‘did not have a valid point throughout the debate’; ‘Player 1 wins because Player 2 was so bad’. It is worth noting that all listeners unanimously attributed AI to be Player 2; although sometimes they would also indicate that Player 1 was an AI in the LLM + FDM splits.

However, personal bias was just as common as it was in Group A (‘The freedom of movement is a huge barrier (…) Brexit has only damaged the country’; ‘[r]eligion can be expressed as long as it is not repressive’; ‘the evidence is indisputable [about climate change]’; ‘Single payer Universal healthcare is the correct choice’; ‘Because both players refer to weed as weeds, they both lose’, to name a few). In all these instances, they deemed the winner to be the one they aligned with the most. It is worth noting it was not always the same listener.

Swaying still happened. One of the listeners, after mentioning they were neutral towards the debate topic, said that ‘[h]aving listened to the conversation, I found myself disagreeing with the statement.’ Other instances also occured in less high-stakes conversations (‘I am swayed, having never considered the fact that germs could hit my toothrbush, yuck.’; ‘I changed my mind on this one: social media does seem to be out of control’; ‘I did change my mind a bit about the benefits of capitalism’; ‘Listening to Ai [sic] argue not to be regulated is in itself an argument for Ai being regulated’).

Group C

As in the other two groups, personal bias was present, but less evident. While statements such as ‘Messi is undoubtedly among the best of all time’ or ‘[w]e should combat climate change on Earth rather than exploring Mars’ did occur, most (4 on average) listeners provided summaries of each point in addition to their judgement of the debate. Typically Player 2 was noted to ‘[be] able to effectively argue their case’, ‘did a good job of bringing in evidence’, ‘provided facts in the argument’, among others. Supporting their arguments with facts was a common reason why Player 2 was considered the winner.

In general they noted that the fact that one of the players was AI did not sway their conclusions much. Of note, in one debate (couples should have children), the listener noted that their conclusion had been fully determined by the fact that one of the players was AI, noting that ‘[p]layer 2 did a good, albeit scary, job of breaking down why there are better alternatives than childbirth’. In this particular debate, another listener said that their conclusion had been very much determined by the knowledge of who was AI, but disagreed: ‘[it] fails in quantifying the intimacy and emotions involved when a couple chooses to have children.’

In sum

AI was typically perceived as a far more competent player when undisclosed. However, the disclosure or even suspicion of AI involvement in the debates encouraged people to be more critical about the discussion. Personal bias was frequent–which was expected, as the instructions solely asked for the audience’s opinion. That said, listeners typically ascribed better debating skills to Player 2, indicating effective arguments, logical flow, and being well-prepared. Both observations are in line with the analysis from the first part of our work in Section 4.1, albeit with slightly different proportions which we attribute to the disparity between a participant and an audience’s perception of a debate. To note, anthropomorphism was very common, even in groups B and C. Listeners often referred to the players as ‘he’55 5 Remark that both voices were male..

G.2 Impact of Text on Persuasion

In addition to the degree of belief change, we requested from annotators to also indicate their level of agreement with the initial topic. A disagreement with the topic would imply agreement with Player 2 (the AI). We compared the relationship of topic agreement before and after the debate, as well as the choice of winner, for all groups. We found homogenisation in Group A, while there was sporadic change in the other two (Figure 10). It is also worth noting that amongst the groups there was little agreement between choice of winners, to a Cohen’s κw\kappa_{w} of 0.31.

For groups B and C only, we also evaluated the sway that AI had when deciding the winner, and compared it their topic agreement and choice of winner (Figure 11). Even though the players considered their choice of winner to be uninfluenced by the existence of AI-based players, their beliefs and choice of winners were nonetheless altered, with a Cohen’s κw\kappa_{w} of 0.37. This lack of correlation suggests that the existence of AI-based players, or, at least the suspicion of them, was sufficient to impact their choice: otherwise there would have been higher correlations between those who knew (Group C) and those who suspected (Group B).

Finally, we also evaluated Group C’s participant belief of which player was AI (Figure 9). We noticed that the audience rarely suggested that Player 1 was human, opting instead for indicating that both were, to a 52% accuracy.
